summary:
Pasco department has no documented trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern on record. It stands under the national framework of Peru.

Under that framework, Law 32331 of 13 May 2025 bars trans people from using public restrooms according to their gender identity, and the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction: its Article 5.1, approved by the plenary of Congress on 2 April 2025 with the second vote waived, prohibits entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than one's birth sex. The underlying bills, 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, presented by legislators including Jorge Montoya and Muñante of Honor y Democracia, also ban inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'; the Comisión de Mujer y Familia approved the merged dictamen unanimously on 20 February 2025, with narrow exceptions for custody and for accompanying minors, the elderly or people with disabilities, and an obligation on venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport.

Human Rights Watch reports that the April 2025 law mandates public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their identity; that its vaguely worded child-protection articles, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content; and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The institute recalls documented cases of trans people barred from public restrooms, including SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissing a trans woman's discrimination complaint against SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI, and notes that gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive. Activist Gianna Camacho argues enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

Legal recognition of gender is partially available. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. A July 2024 report finds hate crimes increasing in Peru with trans women most affected, and co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, states that the recorded numbers are only a sub-registry. A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.

The torture and rape of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León received 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Healthcare classifications have shifted in both directions. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

Hostility is also institutional. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional; and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising. In April 2025 the television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.
tangentialFactors:
Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in its Penal Code. Government Decree Nº 1323 had criminalised discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity with effect from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323; Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, President Kuczynski's veto stood at that point, and the protections were subsequently removed as the Penal Code was reworked. The repeal was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members arguing the President lacked authority to issue the decree, following an April Constitutional Committee vote and a petition carrying one million signatures.

The IDEHPUCP institute invokes Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights, and records dehumanising comparisons made by congressman Lizarzaburu on the floor of Congress.

The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute finds the restroom restriction openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their identity, implicitly casting trans people as harassment risks.
